claim: ICAM-1 concentrates in bile canaliculi and bile ducts of polarized hepatocytes and cholangiocytes in human livers from healthy donors.
source: ICAM-1 concentrates in bile canaliculi (top images) and bile ducts (bottom images) from polarized hepatocytes and cholangiocytes, respectively (arrows), and in sinusoids in human livers from healthy donors.
evidence: Figure 1A shows immunohistochemical staining of ICAM-1 in human liver tissue sections.

claim: CRISPR-CAS9-mediated editing of the ICAM1 gene in HepG2 cells eliminates ICAM-1 expression.
source: CRISPR-CAS9-mediated editing of the ICAM1 gene (ICAM-1_KO) in HepG2 cells. Several clones were selected and pooled to prevent clonal variations.
evidence: Figure 1B shows western blot demonstrating absence of ICAM-1 protein in KO cells compared to WT.

claim: ICAM-1_KO HepG2 cells have enlarged bile canalicular-like structures (eBCs) compared to WT cells.
source: BC area increased from 18.9 ± 1.1 μm2 in WT cells to 51.2 ± 7.2 μm2 in ICAM-1_KO cells. ***p<0.001
evidence: Figure 1E shows quantification of BC area in WT versus ICAM-1_KO cells with statistical significance.

claim: ICAM-1_KO cells proliferate slightly slower than parental WT cells.
source: Cells were seeded at very low density and counted for 96 hr. Bars represent the SD of the mean. n = 3. ** p<0.01.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A shows cell proliferation curves over 96 hours.

claim: ICAM-1_KO cells have similar cell size and percentage of cell death compared to WT cells.
source: In each cell passage, cell density, size (left graph), and percentage of dead cells (right graph) were analyzed in a cell counter Countess 3 (Invitrogen). Bars represent the SD of the mean. n = 5.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows quantification of cell size and death percentage.

claim: Enlarged BCs (eBCs) in ICAM-1_KO cells are enriched in microvilli and sealed by tight junctions.
source: Similar to BCs, eBCs were enriched in microvilli, sealed by tight junctions (TJs), and contained intracellular canalicular markers such as radixin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Text references immunofluorescence data showing TJ and microvilli markers in eBCs.

claim: eBCs in ICAM-1_KO cells do not show significant alterations in the distribution of membrane proteins MDR1 and MRP2.
source: In addition, eBC did not show significant alterations in the distribution of membrane proteins that reach BCs by a direct route of intracellular transport, such as MDR1 and MRP2 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Sai et al., 1999)
evidence: Text references immunofluorescence data and cites previous literature on MDR1 and MRP2 transport.

claim: eBCs in ICAM-1_KO cells retain CD59 distribution similar to normal BCs.
source: In addition, eBC did not show significant alterations in the distribution of membrane proteins that reach BCs by a direct route of intracellular transport, such as MDR1 and MRP2 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Sai et al., 1999), or by an indirect route, such as CD59 (Figure 1D; de Marco et al., 2002).
evidence: Text references immunofluorescence data and cites previous literature on CD59 transport.

claim: eBCs are surrounded by a subapical compartment (SAC) containing plasmolipin and Rab11.
source: eBCs were also surrounded by a subapical compartment (SAC), as observed by detecting endogenous plasmolipin (Cacho-Navas et al., 2022; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) or by expressing the SAC marker GFP-Rab11 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Text references immunofluorescence data showing SAC markers and cites previous work.

claim: Expression of ICAM-1-GFP in ICAM-1_KO cells rescues the enlarged BC phenotype.
source: The enlargement of these canalicular structures was rescued by expressing ICAM-1-GFP in ICAM-1_KO cells, which reduced the size of BCs to those in control HepG2 cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: Figure 1F shows quantification of BC area after ICAM-1-GFP rescue experiment.

claim: ICAM-1 knockdown increases BC area similar to ICAM-1_KO cells.
source: ICAM-1 knockdown (KD) also increased the BC area, confirming the effect of ICAM-1 reduction on BC size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Text references siRNA knockdown experiments with quantification of BC area.

claim: Correlative cryo-SXT reveals that eBCs from ICAM-1_KO cells contain all morphological features of BCs including microvilli abundance and length.
source: Correlative Cryo-SXT revealed that eBCs from ICAM-1_KO cells contained all the morphological features of BCs, although in an enlarged state, including the abundance and length of the microvilli (Figure 1G).
evidence: Figure 1G shows cryo-SXT images of WT and ICAM-1_KO cells.

claim: Potential fusion events between eBCs were observed in ICAM-1_KO cells by Cryo-SXT.
source: Potential fusion events between eBCs were also observed by Cryo-SXT (Figure 2A)
evidence: Figure 2A shows cryo-SXT images of fusing BCs.

claim: Time-lapse fluorescence microscopy shows BC fusion events in ICAM-1_KO cells.
source: Potential fusion events between eBCs were also observed by Cryo-SXT (Figure 2A) and by time-lapse fluorescence microscopy (Figure 2B, left panel, central graph, Videos 1 and 2) in ICAM-1_KO cells.
evidence: Figure 2B shows time-lapse microscopy data and quantification of BC fusion events.

claim: No differences in relative changes in canalicular areas between frames were observed between KO and WT cells in time-lapse experiments.
source: However, no differences in the relative changes in canalicular areas between frames were observed between KO and WT cells in these time-lapse experiments (Figure 2B, right graph).
evidence: Figure 2B right graph shows quantification of BC area changes over time.

claim: Long-term culture of ICAM-1_KO cells induces appearance of microvillus-rich structures much larger than eBCs, covering areas up to 100 μm2.
source: Indeed, long-term culture of ICAM-1_KO (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and ICAM-1_KD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) cells induced the appearance of microvillus-rich structures that were much larger than eBCs observed between 48 and 72 hr, covering areas of up to 100 μm2.
evidence: Text references immunofluorescence data from long-term culture experiments.

claim: Large canalicular structures in long-term cultured ICAM-1_KO cells are surrounded by TJs with cobblestone morphology.
source: These structures were surrounded by TJs with a cobblestone morphology, although the TJ polygons did not enclose an underlying nucleus and, hence, did not correspond to single cells establishing cell–cell contacts (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Figures 2C and 2D show immunofluorescence images of TJ distribution.

claim: Spherical, canalicular-like domains enriched in F-actin are found in contact with large canalicular structures in ICAM-1_KO cells.
source: Spherical, canalicular-like domains enriched in F-actin (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and similar to the BCs observed in control cells were found in contact with these large canalicular structures, suggesting that the fusion of several BCs might contribute to the enlargement of canalicular domains in ICAM-1-depleted cells.
evidence: Text describes immunofluorescence observations and provides interpretation.

claim: Massive eBCs in ICAM-1_KO cells are not exposed to the extracellular milieu as shown by sulfo-NHS-biotin labeling.
source: This revealed that streptavidin did not penetrate the lumens of the eBCs, indicating that these large structures are not exposed to the extracellular milieu (Figure 2E).
evidence: Figure 2E shows surface biotinylation experiment results.

claim: IL-1β, IFN-γ, and the combination of TNF-α and IFN-γ induce ICAM-1 protein expression by a factor of 4-6 in hepatic epithelial cells.
source: IL-1β, IFN-γ, and the combination of TNF-α and IFN-γ induced the expression of ICAM-1 protein by a factor of 4–6, whereas TNF-α had a moderate effect (Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A shows western blot quantification of ICAM-1 expression after cytokine treatment.

claim: Cytokine stimulation causes a greater increase in ICAM-1 expression at basolateral domains compared to apical domains.
source: The quantification of the apical-to-basolateral ratio revealed a greater increase in expression at the basolateral domains compared to the apical ones (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Figures 3B and 3C show quantification and images of ICAM-1 distribution after cytokine treatment.

claim: Cytokine-induced ICAM-1 upregulation correlates with a reduction in the number of BCs.
source: These changes in expression and distribution were correlated with a reduction in the number of BCs in cytokine-stimulated cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: Figure 3D shows quantification of BC frequency after cytokine treatment.

claim: BC loss upon cytokine stimulation is prevented in ICAM-1_KO cells.
source: However, BC loss was prevented when ICAM-1_KO cells were stimulated with these cytokines (Figure 3D, left graphs).
evidence: Figure 3D shows quantification of BC frequency in ICAM-1_KO cells after cytokine treatment.

claim: BC size is not reduced upon cytokine stimulation.
source: In addition, BC size was not reduced upon cytokine stimulation (Figure 3D, right graphs)
evidence: Figure 3D shows quantification of BC area after cytokine treatment.

claim: ICAM-1 expression levels modulate BC size and/or frequency.
source: However, collectively, these findings demonstrate that ICAM-1 expression levels modulate BC size and/or frequency and thus have a role in hepatic epithelial apicobasal polarity.
evidence: Text provides interpretation of the collective experimental findings.

claim: GFP-MLC forms a spherical network that surrounds SirActin-positive BCs.
source: GFP-MLC formed a spherical network that surrounded SirActin-positive BCs (Figure 4A, Video 3).
evidence: Figure 4A shows time-lapse confocal microscopy of GFP-MLC and SirActin.

claim: MLC forms a ring at the base of microvilli-like actin domains but does not localize in the most central parts of microvillar structures.
source: Single planes of the confocal time-lapse projections showed that MLC formed a ring at the base of microvilli-like actin domains, but did not localize in the most central parts of microvillar structures.
evidence: Text describes observations from confocal microscopy analysis.

claim: Active non-muscle myosin-II complexes (p-MLC) are distributed in the most distal parts of BCs where they overlap with F-actin.
source: High-resolution confocal microscopy of endogenous F-actin and myosin light chain phosphorylated in the T18/S19 residues (p-MLC) confirmed that active non-muscle myosin-II complexes were distributed in the most distal parts BC where they overlapped with F-actin, which also formed microvilli-like structures (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows high-resolution confocal microscopy images and quantification.

claim: The regions of F-actin that overlap with ICAM-1 and the actomyosin network clearly differ.
source: In addition, the regions of F-actin that overlapped with ICAM-1 and the actomyosin network clearly differed, and the co-localization of p-MLC and ICAM-1 staining was much less extensive than that of these two proteins with F-actin, as shown by Manders' analyses of the confocal images (Figure 4B, central and right panels).
evidence: Figure 4B shows Manders' colocalization analysis.

claim: Canalicular staining of p-MLC is significantly reduced in ICAM-1_KO cells.
source: Importantly, the canalicular stainings of p-MLC (Figure 4C) and of myosin heavy chain-IIb (MHCIIb) (Figure 4D) were significantly reduced in ICAM-1_KO cells, whereas the F-actin levels were maintained (Figure 4E).
evidence: Figures 4C, 4D, and 4E show immunofluorescence images and quantification.

claim: Canalicular staining of MHCIIb is significantly reduced in ICAM-1_KO cells.
source: Importantly, the canalicular stainings of p-MLC (Figure 4C) and of myosin heavy chain-IIb (MHCIIb) (Figure 4D) were significantly reduced in ICAM-1_KO cells, whereas the F-actin levels were maintained (Figure 4E).
evidence: Figures 4C, 4D, and 4E show immunofluorescence images and quantification.

claim: F-actin levels at BCs are maintained in ICAM-1_KO cells.
source: Importantly, the canalicular stainings of p-MLC (Figure 4C) and of myosin heavy chain-IIb (MHCIIb) (Figure 4D) were significantly reduced in ICAM-1_KO cells, whereas the F-actin levels were maintained (Figure 4E).
evidence: Figure 4E shows quantification of F-actin levels.

claim: F-actin and p-MLC distribution in basolateral membrane domains are higher in ICAM-1_KO cells than in WT cells.
source: In contrast, F-actin and p-MLC distribution in the basolateral membrane domains were higher in ICAM-1_KO cells than that in WT cells (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A show quantification of basolateral protein levels.

claim: Exogenous expression of ICAM-1-GFP in ICAM-1_KO cells restores the canalicular actomyosin network.
source: The exogenous expression of ICAM-GFP in ICAM-1_KO cells restored the canalicular actomyosin network, indicating that ICAM-1 regulates the actomyosin cytoskeleton surrounding BCs (Figure 4C–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figures 4C-E show rescue experiments with ICAM-1-GFP expression.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment induces eBCs similar to those observed in ICAM-1_KO cells.
source: Moreover, cells treated with blebbistatin, the ATPase inhibitor for non-muscle myosin-II, induced eBCs in a manner similar to that observed in ICAM-1_KO cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: Figure 4F shows immunofluorescence images and quantification after blebbistatin treatment.

claim: Blebbistatin prevents ICAM-1-dependent loss of BCs in response to IL-1β.
source: Blebbistatin also prevented the ICAM-1-dependent loss of BCs in response to IL-1β (Figure 4G).
evidence: Figure 4G shows quantification of BC frequency after IL-1β and blebbistatin treatment.

claim: ROCK inhibition with Y27632 phenocopies the effect of ICAM-1 editing and blebbistatin treatment on BC size.
source: ROCK inhibition with Y27632 phenocopied the effect of ICAM-1 editing and blebbistatin treatment on BC size (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1B shows quantification of BC area after Y27632 treatment.

claim: GFP-RhoB and GFP-RhoC significantly concentrate in the plasma membrane of BCs.
source: The expression of GFP-RhoB and GFP-RhoC in polarized hepatic cells suggested that the RhoA subfamily significantly concentrates in the plasma membrane of BCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1C shows fluorescence microscopy of GFP-tagged Rho proteins.

claim: GFP-RhoA expression completely depolarizes hepatic epithelial cells.
source: GFP-RhoA expression completely depolarized these hepatic epithelial cells, so its apicobasal distribution could not be addressed (not shown)
evidence: Text describes observation from expression experiments.

claim: GFP-Rac1 is almost evenly distributed between canalicular and basolateral plasma membrane domains.
source: whereas another Rho GTPase, GFP-Rac1, was almost evenly distributed between canalicular and basolateral plasma membrane domains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1C shows fluorescence microscopy of GFP-Rac1.

claim: BCs concentrate the machinery regulating the Rho-ROCK-actomyosin signaling pathway.
source: Together, these results indicate that BCs concentrate the machinery regulating the Rho-ROCK-actomyosin signaling pathway.
evidence: Text provides interpretation of the collective experimental findings on Rho GTPases and actomyosin.

claim: Cells seeded on anti-ICAM-1 antibody-coated coverslips are unable to form BCs after 24 hr of culture.
source: Cells seeded on anti-ICAM-1 antibody-coated coverslips were unable to form BCs after 24 hr of culture and had more stress fibers than did cells seeded on surfaces coated with control immunoglobulin(Ig)-G, anti-transferrin receptor (TfR) or the integrin ligand, fibronectin, all of which formed BCs with a frequency similar to that of cells plated on uncoated surfaces (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Figures 5A-C show immunofluorescence images and quantification of BC formation on different coated surfaces.

claim: Cells on anti-ICAM-1 antibodies have more stress fibers than cells on control surfaces.
source: Cells seeded on anti-ICAM-1 antibody-coated coverslips were unable to form BCs after 24 hr of culture and had more stress fibers than did cells seeded on surfaces coated with control immunoglobulin(Ig)-G, anti-transferrin receptor (TfR) or the integrin ligand, fibronectin, all of which formed BCs with a frequency similar to that of cells plated on uncoated surfaces (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Figures 5A-C show immunofluorescence images and quantification of stress fibers.

claim: Cells on anti-ICAM-1 antibodies frequently display stellate stress fibers similar to those arising in response to constitutively active ROCK.
source: Moreover, cells on anti-ICAM-1 antibodies frequently displayed stellate stress fibers that were similar to those arising in response to the expression of the constitutively active mutant of ROCK (Figure 5A–C; Garg et al., 2008; Nakano et al., 1999).
evidence: Figures 5A-C show immunofluorescence images and quantification; text cites previous literature on ROCK-induced stress fibers.

claim: Stellate stress fibers concentrate surface ICAM-1 in their proximities.
source: We found that in addition to the fraction of receptor localized on the basal surface after 24 hr of adhesion, stellate stress fibers concentrated surface ICAM-1 in their proximities (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A show immunofluorescence images of ICAM-1 distribution.

claim: p-MLC localizes at F-actin-rich regions where stellate stress fibers arise.
source: whereas p-MLC localized at the F-actin-rich regions where stellate stress fibers arise (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A show immunofluorescence images of p-MLC distribution.

claim: Stellate stress fibers do not constitute aberrant BCs as they lack canalicular morphology and do not concentrate MDR1.
source: These cellular structures did not constitute aberrant BCs since they neither had a canalicular morphology nor concentrated other canalicular markers such as MDR1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows immunofluorescence images of MDR1 distribution.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment restores canalicular morphogenesis in cells seeded on anti-ICAM-1-coated coverslips.
source: When cells seeded on anti-ICAM-1-coated coverslips were treated with blebbistatin, canalicular morphogenesis was restored to a level comparable with that observed in ICAM-1_KO cells on anti-ICAM-1 antibody-coated coverslips or in cells cultured on control coverslips (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figures 5B and 5C show immunofluorescence images and quantification after blebbistatin treatment.

claim: Impairment of BC formation in response to surface ICAM-1 immobilization depends on non-muscle myosin-II.
source: This implies that the impairment of BC formation in response to surface ICAM-1 immobilization depends on non-muscle myosin-II.
evidence: Text provides interpretation of blebbistatin rescue experiments.

claim: Blebbistatin affects only the distribution of MLC and not the phosphorylation of T18/S19 residues.
source: As previously described, the myosin inhibitor blebbistatin affected only the distribution of MLC (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), and not the phosphorylation of the residues recognized by the antibody (Ponsaerts et al., 2008; Calaminus et al., 2007).
evidence: Figure 5B shows immunofluorescence images; text cites previous literature on blebbistatin effects.

claim: Overall signaling to p-MLC in cells plated on anti-ICAM-1 antibodies is similar to that of cells on fibronectin.
source: In addition, the overall signaling to p-MLC in cells plated on anti-ICAM-1 antibodies was similar to that of cells on FN (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1C shows western blot analysis of p-MLC levels.

claim: Impaired morphogenesis upon ICAM-1 immobilization is specific to ICAM-1 and independent of general actin remodeling during cell adhesion.
source: indicating that the impaired morphogenesis was specific to ICAM-1 immobilization, and independent of the general actin remodeling and myosin-II activation occurring in response to the adhesion and spreading of cells previously in suspension.
evidence: Text provides interpretation of p-MLC quantification data.

claim: ICAM-1 surface engagement by clustering with a secondary antibody induces phosphorylation of MLC.
source: Indeed, ICAM-1 surface engagement by clustering with a secondary antibody, independently of epithelial adhesion and spreading, was sufficient to induce the phosphorylation of MLC (Figure 5E)
evidence: Figure 5E shows western blot analysis of p-MLC levels after ICAM-1 clustering.

claim: ICAM-1 signals to actomyosin in hepatic epithelial cells.
source: which demonstrates that the receptor signals to actomyosin in these cells.
evidence: Text provides interpretation of ICAM-1 clustering experiment.

claim: ICAM-1_KO cells have impaired ability to interact with T cells.
source: First, ICAM-1_KO cells had also impaired their ability to interact with T cells, confirming the essential role of epithelial ICAM-1 in T-cell adhesion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1D shows quantification of T-cell adhesion.

claim: Co-culture of T-lymphocytes with polarized HepG2 cells for at least 6 hr reduces the number of BCs by approximately 40%.
source: In addition, co-culture of T-lymphocytes with polarized HepG2 cells for at least 6 hr, at an approximate ratio of 1:2, reduced the number of BCs found in cells prior to adhesion by approximately 40%.
evidence: Text describes quantification of BC frequency after T-cell co-culture.

claim: Signaling events that control epithelial apicobasal polarity by ICAM-1 in the absence of immune cells also mediate reduction in polarity upon leukocyte adhesion.
source: Hence, these results indicate that the signaling events that control epithelial apicobasal polarity by ICAM-1 in the absence of interaction with immune cells also mediate the reduction in epithelial polarity and BC frequency upon leukocyte adhesion (Figure 5F).
evidence: Figure 5F shows quantification of BC frequency after T-cell co-culture; text provides interpretation.

claim: Hepatic ICAM-1 signaling to actomyosin controls canalicular morphogenesis and frequency.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that hepatic ICAM-1 signaling to actomyosin controls canalicular morphogenesis and frequency (Figure 5G).
evidence: Text provides interpretation of collective experimental findings; Figure 5G shows model diagram.

claim: BioID analysis identified EBP50/NHERF1/SLC9A3R1 in the proximity interactome of ICAM-1.
source: Two independent experiments revealed a restricted set of proteins that were biotinylated in both assays and only in cells expressing the ICAM-1-BirA* chimera. Amongst them, the ezrin-radixin-moesin phosphoprotein (EBP)-50/NHERF1/SLC9A3R1 was detected and further validated (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Figure 6A shows BioID pull-down and western blot validation.

claim: EBP50 is highly polarized and concentrates and colocalizes with ICAM-1 in BCs.
source: We found that EBP50 was highly polarized and concentrated and colocalized with ICAM-1 in BCs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Figure 6B shows immunofluorescence images and Manders' colocalization analysis.

claim: EBP50 has a sinusoidal and canalicular distribution in murine hepatic tissue.
source: Confocal analysis of hepatic tissue also revealed a sinusoidal (S) and canalicular (red arrows) distribution of EBP50 in vivo (Figure 6C).
evidence: Figure 6C shows immunofluorescence images of liver tissue sections.

claim: EBP50 is exclusively localized in actin-positive canalicular microvilli but not in the peripheral actomyosin mesh.
source: However, triple co-staining revealed that EBP50 was exclusively localized in the actin-positive canalicular microvilli but not in the peripheral actomyosin mesh (Figure 6D).
evidence: Figure 6D shows triple immunofluorescence staining and intensity distribution analysis.

claim: Full-length EBP50 shows weak interaction with ICAM-1 in immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Immunoprecipitation experiments showed a weak interaction between ICAM-1 and ectopically expressed full-length EBP50, which was strongly increased when the two N-terminal PDZ domains were expressed alone, without the masking C-terminal EB domain (Figure 6E).
evidence: Figure 6E shows immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis.

claim: The two N-terminal PDZ domains of EBP50 show strongly increased interaction with ICAM-1 compared to full-length EBP50.
source: Immunoprecipitation experiments showed a weak interaction between ICAM-1 and ectopically expressed full-length EBP50, which was strongly increased when the two N-terminal PDZ domains were expressed alone, without the masking C-terminal EB domain (Figure 6E).
evidence: Figure 6E shows immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis.

claim: EBP50 binding to ICAM-1 shows preferential interaction with the second PDZ domain.
source: The binding of EBP50 fragments containing only one PDZ domain was clearly reduced and suggested a preferential interaction with the second PDZ domain.
evidence: Text describes results from immunoprecipitation experiments with PDZ domain fragments.

claim: Expression of PDZ domains is sufficient to target EBP50 to BCs.
source: The expression of these PDZ domains was sufficient to target EBP50 to BCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1E shows immunofluorescence images of PDZ domain localization.

claim: ICAM-1 and EBP50 form overlapping nano-scale domains along F-actin-rich microvilli as revealed by STED microscopy.
source: STED revealed that both ICAM-1 and EBP50 distribution was not even, but displayed patterns of overlapping nano-scale domains along F-actin-rich microvilli. These nanodomains had a size between 80 and 200 nm.
evidence: Text describes STED microscopy observations.

claim: Microvillar F-actin does not form nanoscopic clusters in filaments as shown by super-resolution imaging.
source: In contrast, super-resolution images showed that microvillar F-actin did not form nanoscopic clusters in these filaments (Figure 6G).
evidence: Figure 6G shows STED microscopy images of F-actin distribution.

claim: In non-polarized cells with few microvilli, ICAM-1 is more evenly distributed and does not overlap with EBP50.
source: Furthermore, in plasma membrane regions containing few microvilli, such as those of non-polarized cells, ICAM-1 was more evenly distributed and did not overlap with EBP50 (Figure 6H).
evidence: Figure 6H shows STED microscopy images of non-polarized cells.

claim: EBP50 nanodomains aggregate in response to ICAM-1 engagement, forming circular structures that partially overlap with clustered receptor.
source: These EBP50 nanodomains, however, responded to ICAM-1 engagement by aggregating themselves, often forming circular structures of several nanoclusters, which only partially overlapped with the clustered receptor (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: Figures 6H and 6I show STED microscopy images and Manders' analysis after ICAM-1 engagement.

claim: ICAM-1 engagement induces changes in EBP50 condensation properties, increasing its insolubility to mild non-ionic detergents.
source: Such redistribution caused EBP50 to become more insoluble to mild-non-ionic detergents (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), indicating that ICAM-1 induces changes in the condensation properties of EBP50, either by increasing the association of EBP50 to cytoskeletal structures or by changing its oligomerization properties (Fouassier et al., 2000).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1F shows western blot analysis of soluble and insoluble fractions; text cites previous literature.

claim: ICAM-1 and EBP50 nanoclusters are in closer proximity in apical BCs than in non-polarized plasma membrane regions.
source: Importantly, ICAM-1 and EBP50 nanoclusters were in closer proximity in apical BCs than in non-polarized plasma membrane regions, even if non-polarized cells were exposed to anti-ICAM-1 antibody, which increased nanocluster overlapping, as shown by Manders' analyses (Figure 6I).
evidence: Figure 6I shows Manders' colocalization analysis comparing apical and non-polarized regions.

claim: Proximal interaction and potential ICAM-1-EBP50-mediated signaling mainly occur in BCs in the absence of receptor engagement.
source: This indicates that the proximal interaction and the potential ICAM-1-EBP50-mediated signaling mainly occur in BCs in the absence of receptor engagement.
evidence: Text provides interpretation of Manders' colocalization analysis.

claim: ICAM-1 signals and reorganizes EBP50 in macromolecular complexes that do not contain the receptor.
source: In addition, it also suggests that, in addition to associating to this scaffold protein, ICAM-1 also signals and reorganizes EBP50 in macromolecular complexes that do not contain the receptor.
evidence: Text provides interpretation of STED microscopy observations.

claim: Absence of ICAM-1 in KO cells causes no overall dispersion of EBP50 from BCs.
source: The absence of ICAM-1 in KO cells caused no overall dispersion of EBP50 from BCs, indicating that EBP50 is localized in these apical plasma membrane domains through additional interactions (Figure 6J).
evidence: Figure 6J shows immunofluorescence images and quantification of EBP50 intensity.

claim: ICAM-1_KO cells show increased intensity of EBP50 nanodomains but not changes in their distribution and density.
source: Nevertheless, quantification of EBP50 by STED microscopy revealed an increase in the intensity of the nanodomains in ICAM-1_KO cells with respect to WT, but not in their distribution and density, measured by analyzing the nearest-neighbor distance (Figure 6K, nnd).
evidence: Figure 6K shows STED microscopy images and quantification of nanodomain intensity and nearest-neighbor distance.

claim: EBP50 nanoclustering does not require ICAM-1 expression, but ICAM-1 modulates EBP50 clustering at BCs.
source: These observations suggest that EBP50 nanoclustering does not require ICAM-1 expression, but also that the receptor modulates EBP50 clustering at BCs.
evidence: Text provides interpretation of STED microscopy quantification.

claim: siRNA-mediated SLC9A3R1 gene silencing reduces EBP50 expression by around 50% and increases BC area by almost half.
source: siRNA-mediated SLC9A3R1 gene silencing reduced EBP50 expression by around 50% and increased BC area by almost half (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Figures 7A and 7B show western blot and immunofluorescence quantification after EBP50 knockdown.

claim: EBP50 depletion moderately decreases pMLC staining at the canalicular actomyosin network.
source: Although moderately, this EBP50 depletion decreased pMLC staining at the canalicular actomyosin network.
evidence: Text describes quantification of pMLC levels after EBP50 knockdown.

claim: F-actin levels at canalicular microvilli of EBP50_KD cells are lower than in control cells.
source: Unlike ICAM-1_KO cells, F-actin levels at the canalicular microvilli of EBP50_KD cells were lower than that in control cells, which suggests that EBP50 has functions that are independent of ICAM-1 in these apical domains (Figure 7B).
evidence: Figure 7B shows immunofluorescence quantification of F-actin levels.

claim: EBP50 depletion attenuates the negative effect of ICAM-1 on BC morphogenesis.
source: It is particularly noteworthy that EBP50 depletion attenuated the negative effect of ICAM-1 on BC morphogenesis and ICAM-1-mediated signaling to F-actin (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: Figures 7C-E show immunofluorescence images and quantification after EBP50 knockdown and ICAM-1 immobilization.

claim: EBP50_KD cells form more BCs upon ICAM-1 immobilization compared to control cells.
source: EBP50_KD cells formed more BCs upon ICAM-1 immobilization and reduced the number of stress fibers with respect to control cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: Figure 7E shows quantification of BC frequency and stress fibers.

claim: EBP50 accumulates with ICAM-1 close to stellate stress fibers.
source: In addition, EBP50 accumulated with ICAM-1 close to stellate stress fibers, consistent with the interaction between ICAM-1 and EBP50 in membrane domains enriched in underlying F-actin (Figure 7D, top images).
evidence: Figure 7D shows immunofluorescence images of EBP50 and ICAM-1 distribution.

claim: EBP50 regulates ICAM-1-mediated signaling toward actomyosin.
source: These results indicate that EBP50 regulates ICAM-1-mediated signaling toward actomyosin.
evidence: Text provides interpretation of EBP50 knockdown experiments.

claim: ICAM-1 is highly expressed in hepatic sinusoids and with less intensity in bile canaliculi and ducts in murine livers.
source: A confocal analysis of ICAM-1 distribution in murine livers revealed that this receptor was highly expressed in hepatic sinusoids and, with less intensity, in bile canaliculi and ducts (Figure 8A; Colás-Algora et al., 2020).
evidence: Figure 8A shows immunofluorescence images of murine liver tissue; text cites previous work.

claim: Livers from ICAM-1_KO mice show a significant increase in canalicular width compared to WT littermates.
source: Hence, we performed a morphological study of BC in livers from ICAM-1_KO mice and their WT littermates (Bullard et al., 2007), which revealed a significant increase in canalicular width in hepatic tissue lacking ICAM-1 expression (Figure 8B).
evidence: Figure 8B shows immunofluorescence images and quantification of BC width in murine liver tissue; text cites mouse model reference.

claim: Canalicular components F-actin and MRP2 are still detected in BCs from ICAM-1_KO livers.
source: Canalicular components such as F-actin and MRP2 were still detected in BC from ICAM-1_KO livers, consistently with the results observed in human hepatic cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: Figure 8C shows immunohistochemical analysis of murine liver tissue.

claim: Murine hepatic organoids express albumin and ICAM-1 without previous exposure to inflammatory stimuli.
source: Murine hepatic organoids expressed hepatocyte markers such as albumin. They also expressed ICAM-1 without previous exposure to inflammatory stimuli (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B; Broutier et al., 2016; Huch et al., 2013).
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1B shows PCR analysis; text cites previous literature on organoid characterization.

claim: Hepatic organoids form spheroids of cell aggregates with cell-cell junctions.
source: Hepatic organoids had a heterogeneous morphology but mostly formed spheroids of cell aggregates that formed cell–cell junctions (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 8D shows immunofluorescence images of organoid morphology.

claim: The bile canalicular marker HA-4 localizes between cells in peripheral regions of hepatic organoid spheroids.
source: Interestingly, the bile canalicular marker HA-4 was localized between cells in the peripheral regions of these spheroids. HA-4 exhibited a staining pattern of wide tubular and dotted domains different from that of the cell–cell junction marker ZO-1 (Figure 8D, enlarged areas).
evidence: Figure 8D shows immunofluorescence images of HA-4 and ZO-1 distribution.

claim: Time-lapse analysis of CFDA shows fluorescent CF is laterally secreted between cells in hepatic organoids.
source: Moreover, a time-lapse analysis of carboxyfluorescein diacetate (CFDA), a fluorescent probe of hepatobiliary transport and secretion into the bile canaliculi, revealed that fluorescent CF was also laterally secreted between cells, as shown by the relative distribution of CF with respect to the nuclei, which was similar to that of HA-4 (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: Figures 8D and 8E show time-lapse fluorescence microscopy of CFDA secretion.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy reveals lateral cavities between cells in hepatic organoids that are sealed by electrodense cell-cell junctions and contain long, thin microvilli.
source: Transmission electron microscopy of these organoids revealed the existence of lateral cavities between cells, which were sealed by electrodense cell–cell junctions and contained long, thin microvilli, different from those observed in the plasma membrane domain facing bigger lumens in the central part of the spheroids (Figure 8F).
evidence: Figure 8F shows transmission electron microscopy images.

claim: Cell-cell junctions in lateral lumens of hepatic organoids resemble membrane bulkheads that contribute to canalicular lumen elongation.
source: The cell–cell junctions observed in these lateral lumens resembled the recently described membrane bulkheads that contribute to the elongation of canalicular lumens (Figure 8F, bottom-right image) (Belicova et al., 2021).
evidence: Figure 8F shows electron microscopy images; text cites previous literature on membrane bulkheads.

claim: Differentiated hepatic organoids form BC-like lateral cavities that morphologically and functionally resemble BCs.
source: Collectively, these results suggested that differentiated hepatic organoids form BC-like lateral cavities that morphologically and functionally resemble BCs.
evidence: Text provides interpretation of organoid characterization data.

claim: ICAM-1 accumulates in BC-like lateral domains in mouse and human hepatic organoids.
source: Interestingly, ICAM-1 accumulated in these domains in mouse and human hepatic organoids (Figure 8G).
evidence: Figure 8G shows immunofluorescence images of ICAM-1 distribution in organoids.

claim: pMLC and EBP50 localize in lateral plasma membrane domains of hepatic organoids.
source: pMLC and EBP50 were also localized in lateral plasma membrane domains, although EBP50 also concentrated in the plasma membrane facing central lumens (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1C shows immunofluorescence images of pMLC and EBP50 distribution.

claim: ICAM-1_KO differentiated organoids have larger BC-like lateral lumen areas than WT organoids.
source: To address whether ICAM-1 regulates the morphology of these BC-like lateral cavities, we generated hepatic organoids from WT and ICAM-1_KO mice. Measuring the area of BC-like lateral lumens revealed larger areas in ICAM-1_KO than that in WT-differentiated organoids (Figure 8H).
evidence: Figure 8H shows electron microscopy images and quantification of lateral lumen area.

claim: BC-like lateral domains are functional in WT and ICAM-1_KO organoids as shown by CFDA time-lapse and albumin secretion assays.
source: Time-lapse analyses of organoids incubated with CFDA (Figure 8I, top) as well as albumin secretion assays (Figure 8I, bottom), indicated that BC-like lateral domains were functional in WT and ICAM-1_KO organoids.
evidence: Figure 8I shows time-lapse microscopy and albumin secretion quantification.

claim: ICAM-1_KO organoids contain enlarged cells.
source: In addition, confocal (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D and E) and electron (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F) microscopy analyses also revealed that ICAM-1_KO organoids contained enlarged cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1D-G show microscopy images and quantification of cell size.

claim: ICAM-1 may exert overall control of submembranal cytoskeletal scaffolds that control cellular size in hepatic organoids.
source: suggesting that ICAM-1 may exert an overall control of the submembranal cytoskeletal scaffolds that control cellular size in the hepatic organoids.
evidence: Text provides interpretation of cell size observations in ICAM-1_KO organoids.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment increases the area of lateral lumens in hepatic organoids similar to ICAM-1_KO organoids.
source: Finally, incubation with blebbistatin also increased the area of these lateral lumens in a manner almost identical to that observed in ICAM-1_KO organoids (Figure 8J).
evidence: Figure 8J shows electron microscopy images and quantification after blebbistatin treatment.

claim: ICAM-1 is organized in nano-scale domains in surface microvilli at BCs.
source: Hence, collectively, our observations from the various polarized hepatic cellular models reveal that ICAM-1 is organized in nano-scale domains in surface microvilli at BCs
evidence: Text provides summary interpretation of STED microscopy findings.

claim: ICAM-1 signals to actomyosin from BCs independent of its role as an adhesion receptor for immune cells.
source: from where the receptor signals to actomyosin, independent of its role as an adhesion receptor for immune cells.
evidence: Text provides summary interpretation of experimental findings.

claim: Apical confinement of ICAM-1 regulates BC size and hepatic cell architecture.
source: This apical confinement of ICAM-1 regulates BC size and the hepatic cell architecture.
evidence: Text provides summary interpretation of experimental findings.

claim: There is a close and reciprocal connection between epithelial apicobasal polarity and inflammatory response through ICAM-1.
source: In a more general perspective and taking into account previous reports (Reglero-Real et al., 2014; Cacho-Navas et al., 2022), these findings also provide direct evidence of a close and reciprocal connection between epithelial apicobasal polarity and the inflammatory response through ICAM-1 (Figure 9).
evidence: Text provides interpretation citing previous work; Figure 9 shows model diagram.

claim: ICAM-1 is the counterreceptor of leukocyte β2-integrins and mediates firm adhesion of leukocytes to epithelial and endothelial cells.
source: Intercellular adhesion molecule (ICAM)-1 is the counterreceptor of leukocyte β2-integrins and mediates firm adhesion of leukocytes to epithelial and endothelial cells (Rothlein et al., 1986; Sumagin et al., 2014; Reglero-Real et al., 2012; Vestweber, 2015).
evidence: Text cites multiple previous studies establishing ICAM-1 function.

claim: ICAM-1 signals and remodels the plasma membrane and underlying actin cytoskeleton to promote transendothelial migration.
source: ICAM-1 is not only a passive endothelial surface anchor for circulating immune cells, but also signals and remodels the plasma membrane and the underlying actin cytoskeleton to promote transendothelial migration (TEM) and extravasation of leukocytes in many inflammatory diseases (Reglero-Real et al., 2012)
evidence: Text cites previous work on ICAM-1 signaling function.

claim: Inhibition of ICAM-1 function reduces liver injury in cholestasis.
source: including those involving cholestasis, in which inhibition of ICAM-1 function reduces liver injury (Gujral et al., 2004).
evidence: Text cites previous study on ICAM-1 in cholestasis.

claim: ICAM-1 is apically confined in polarized intestinal and hepatic epithelia.
source: ICAM-1 is apically confined in polarized intestinal and hepatic epithelia (Sumagin et al., 2014; Reglero-Real et al., 2014; Reglero-Real et al., 2016)
evidence: Text cites previous studies on ICAM-1 localization.

claim: Apical ICAM-1 confinement confers capacity to establish a haptotactic gradient to guide infiltrated immune cells.
source: which confers on these cellular barriers the capacity to establish a haptotactic gradient between apical and basolateral membrane domains in order to guide infiltrated immune cells (Sumagin et al., 2014).
evidence: Text cites previous work on ICAM-1 function in immune cell guidance.

claim: The filamentous actin cytoskeleton in bile canaliculus forms microvilli containing actin but not myosin.
source: The filamentous actin cytoskeleton in the bile canaliculus forms small membrane protrusions, called microvilli, which contain actin but not myosin.
evidence: Text describes established knowledge about canalicular cytoskeleton.

claim: An actomyosin mesh surrounds the basal regions of canalicular microvilli and regulates bile canaliculus diameter and dynamics.
source: However, early electron microscopy analyses and studies of bile canaliculus dynamics in vivo revealed the additional existence of an actomyosin mesh surrounding the basal regions of these microvilli. This cytoskeletal scaffold regulates the diameter and dynamics of the biliary network and is involved in bile trafficking and cholestasis (Meyer et al., 2020; Tsukada et al., 1995; Gupta et al., 2017).
evidence: Text cites previous studies on canalicular actomyosin.

claim: Hepatic ICAM-1 in bile canaliculi and ducts is not accessible to circulating immune cells.
source: The population of hepatic ICAM-1 molecules that are segregated into bile canaliculi and ducts is not accessible to circulating immune cells, which are in contact with the basolateral membranes of hepatic epithelial cells through the space of Disse.
evidence: Text describes anatomical relationship between ICAM-1 localization and immune cell access.

claim: Leukocyte adhesion increases when hepatic epithelial cells lose polarity and expose the apical ICAM-1 receptor pool.
source: Indeed, the adhesion of leukocytes increases when these epithelial cells lose their polarity and expose this receptor pool.
evidence: Text describes relationship between polarity and leukocyte adhesion.

claim: Basolateral ICAM-1 is highly dynamic, but the apical pool is highly stable and confined within BCs.
source: Studies of ICAM-1 dynamics have demonstrated that basolateral ICAM-1 is highly dynamic, but the apical pool of receptors is highly stable and confined within BCs (Reglero-Real et al., 2014).
evidence: Text cites previous work on ICAM-1 dynamics.

claim: ICAM-1 confinement in BCs depends on interaction with underlying canalicular F-actin.
source: This confinement depends on the interaction of ICAM-1 with the underlying canalicular F-actin (Reglero-Real et al., 2014).
evidence: Text cites previous work on ICAM-1-actin interaction.

claim: EBP50 is a scaffolding protein that interacts with Rho and Rab GTPase activity regulators.
source: EBP50 is a scaffolding protein that interacts with Rho and Rab GTPase activity regulators (Hsu et al., 2010; Reczek and Bretscher, 2001)
evidence: Text cites previous studies on EBP50 function.

claim: EBP50 can bind directly to transmembrane proteins or indirectly through interaction with ERM proteins.
source: and can bind directly to transmembrane proteins or indirectly through the interaction with ERM proteins, which in turn also bind to Ig-superfamily receptors (Barreiro et al., 2002; Reglero-Real et al., 2014).
evidence: Text cites previous studies on EBP50 binding mechanisms.

claim: EBP50 has been found to interact with ICAM-1 in whole rat hepatic tissue and regulate liver inflammatory response after bile duct ligation.
source: EBP50 has been found to interact with ICAM-1 in whole rat hepatic tissue and regulate the liver inflammatory response after bile duct ligation, although the precise molecular mechanisms underlying such regulation, and the cellular identity and localization where such interaction takes place, have not been addressed (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Text cites previous study on ICAM-1-EBP50 interaction in liver injury model.

claim: EBP50 is maintained in a closed conformation by head-to-tail intramolecular interaction that masks its association with ligands through PDZ domains.
source: EBP50 is a modular protein that is maintained in a closed conformation by a head-to-tail intramolecular interaction that masks its association with ligands through its two N-terminal PDZ domains (Morales et al., 2007).
evidence: Text cites previous study on EBP50 structure and regulation.
